blocks.text: When microbes attack, macrophages give the immediate response by engulfing them. This cannot eliminate many microbes, but it gives the immune system time to respond. A macrophage that engulfs a microbe also produces special proteins for helper T cells; when helper T cells recognise these through their receptors they are activated and start two parallel responses: cell-mediated immunity and antibody-mediated immunity.

Cell-mediated immunity, carried out by T cells, protects against virus infections and cancer by killing abnormal or virus-infected cells. Cytotoxic T cells recognise and destroy infected body cells, killing as natural killer cells do, by puncturing the membranes of the target cells.

blocks.alt: Top: a macrophage showing special proteins activates a helper T cell, which starts two responses. Below, six numbered boxes: 1 proliferation into clones of T cells, 2 activation calling macrophages, 3 induction in the thymus, 4 attack by cytotoxic T cells that make infected cells burst, 5 suppression by suppressor T cells after 1-2 weeks, 6 memory T cells.
blocks.caption: Events in cell-mediated immunity (original diagram after Figure 21.12).
blocks.long_description: When a macrophage engulfs a microbe it produces special proteins that activate helper T cells, which start cell-mediated and antibody-mediated immunity. In cell-mediated immunity: 1, the helper T cell releases T cell growth factor, and large clones of T cells form; 2, a second factor attracts macrophages to the site; 3, helper T cells activate inducer T cells in the thymus, which mature more T cells; 4, cytotoxic T cells bind infected cells and disrupt their membranes so they burst; 5, suppressor T cells, slower to multiply, shut the response down after 1-2 weeks; 6, memory helper and cytotoxic T cells remain, probably for life, for a rapid response later.

items: Proliferation: the activated helper T cell produces soluble chemicals such as T cell growth factor, which starts the proliferation of all types of T cells into large clones able to recognise the antigen.
Activation: a second factor from the helper T cell attracts macrophages to the site of infection.
Induction: helper T cells activate inducer T cells in the thymus, which trigger the maturation of lymphocytes into T cells.
Attack: receptors on cytotoxic T cells recognise infected body cells; the T cells bind them and disrupt their membranes, and the cells burst.
Suppression: suppressor T cells block the cytotoxic response. They multiply more slowly, so at first they cannot stop the attack, but after 1 to 2 weeks they are numerous enough to shut it down.
Memory: a population of helper and cytotoxic T cells, the memory cells, persists, probably for life, and gives a rapid response to any later encounter with the microbe.

blocks.text: The stimulated helper T cell also activates a second, stronger defence, antibody-mediated or humoral immunity, whose key players are the B cells. B cells do not attack antigens directly; they mark them for destruction, and they also inactivate toxic molecules.

blocks.alt: Top: a B cell with receptors binds an antigen, a helper T cell signals it, it divides into a clone of plasma cells, and they secrete Y-shaped antibodies. Middle: three ways antibody-coated antigens are destroyed, by complement, by a macrophage and by killer cells. Bottom: suppression and memory boxes.
blocks.caption: Events in antibody-mediated immunity (original diagram after Figure 21.13).
blocks.long_description: Each B cell binds antigen through the B receptor proteins on its surface. Helper T cells bind these antigen-bound B cells and release proteins that make them proliferate into many plasma cells. Most plasma cells stop dividing and make and secrete B receptor proteins, now called antibodies, in large numbers within a few days. Antibodies mark antigens for destruction: some activate complement proteins that make holes in the antigen cell so it bursts; some are recognised by macrophages, which ingest the coated antigen; and killer cells with receptors for antibody-coated antigens bind and kill them. After several weeks suppressor T cells shut the response down, and memory B cells remain to give a rapid secondary response, which is how vaccines work.

items: Proliferation: each B cell binds antigen through the B receptor proteins on its surface; helper T cells bind these B cells and release proteins that make them proliferate into many plasma cells.

Differentiation and secretion: most plasma cells stop reproducing and make more B receptor proteins, which are secreted and are now called antibodies; plasma cells secrete huge numbers of antibodies in a few days.

Attack: antibodies mark an antigen for destruction in one of three ways: some activate complement proteins, which make holes in the antibody-coated cell so water enters and it bursts; some are recognised by macrophages, which ingest the antigen; and killer cells, like NK cells but with receptors for antibody-coated antigens, bind and kill them.
Suppression: after several weeks suppressor T cells shut down the antibody response.
Memory: some members of the clone of plasma cells do not produce antibodies; they persist as memory B cells and give a rapid secondary response to any later encounter with the same antigen.

blocks.title: Vaccines and antibodies
blocks.text: A vaccine, made from killed or weakened pathogens, stimulates antibody production and the formation of memory cells. Antibodies make up about 20% by weight of the total protein in blood plasma.

blocks.title: Immune system and gene therapy
blocks.text: Malignant melanoma is a lethal skin cancer. Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) attack tumours but are not strong enough to control them. Genetic engineers are trying to insert a gene into TILs so that they make tumour necrosis factor (TNF), a protein that kills tumour cells, and then return them to the patient's blood to enter the tumour.

An antibody is a Y-shaped protein of four polypeptide chains, two identical long (heavy) chains and two short (light) chains, held together by disulfide bridges. Each chain has a constant region, similar in all antibodies of the same class, and a variable region that differs among antibodies. The variable regions of one heavy and one light chain on each arm of the Y form a specific binding site. Because different antibodies have different variable regions, antibodies are specific: each destroys the antigen that stimulated its production.

blocks.alt: A large Y shape. Two long blue heavy chains form the stem and run up the inner side of each arm; two shorter green light chains lie along the outer side of the arms. Orange tips on all four chains are the variable regions, yellow bars are disulfide bridges, and red circles at the ends of the arms are antigens in the binding sites.
blocks.caption: Structure of an antibody (original diagram after Figure 21.14).
blocks.long_description: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein of four polypeptide chains: two identical long (heavy) chains and two short (light) chains, held together by disulfide bridges. Each chain has a constant region, similar in all antibodies of one class, and a variable region that differs among antibodies. The variable regions of one heavy and one light chain at the tip of each arm form a specific antigen-binding site. Because different antibodies have different variable regions, each is specific for the antigen that stimulated it.

blocks.text: Only a small part of an antigen molecule, its determinant, fits an antibody's binding site. When many different antibodies attach to one antigen, each at a different part of its surface, they are polyclonal antibodies. Antibodies that attach to only one determinant are monoclonal antibodies.

In 1984 Cesar Milstein and Georges Kohler received the Nobel Prize for learning how to produce monoclonal antibodies. They mixed antibody-producing plasma cells with cancer cells called myelomas and found new cells growing and dividing, the hybridomas, which used the plasma cell's genes to make antibodies and the myeloma's genes to grow and divide. The hybridomas kept producing the antibody in which their plasma cell had specialised.

blocks.alt: Top left: an antigen with four different determinants, each bound by a differently coloured antibody (polyclonal). Top right: identical antibodies binding only one determinant (monoclonal). Bottom: a plasma cell plus a myeloma cell fuse into a hybridoma, which grows and divides in culture and releases monoclonal antibodies.
blocks.caption: Polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies and hybridomas (original diagram after Figure 21.15).
blocks.long_description: Only a small part of an antigen, its determinant, fits an antibody's binding site. When many different antibodies bind one antigen, each at a different determinant, they are polyclonal; antibodies that bind only one determinant are monoclonal. Milstein and Kohler, awarded the Nobel Prize in 1984, mixed antibody-making plasma cells with cancer cells called myelomas and obtained hybridomas, which used the plasma cell's genes to make one antibody and the myeloma's genes to keep dividing. Monoclonal antibodies are used to purify particular molecules, as interferon was purified, to deliver therapies, and in research on carrying radioactivity to cancer cells.

blocks.text: Monoclonal antibodies are important because they can purify specific molecules from complex mixtures; interferon was purified this way. In medicine they are used as vehicles to deliver specific therapies, and research is under way on antigens found only on cancer cells, against which radioactive monoclonal antibodies could be aimed to kill cancer cells selectively.
